raw_text:
# Transcaval Access for Structural Heart Interventions: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The expansion of transcatheter therapies for structural heart disease has created a growing demand for large-bore vascular access in patients who lack adequate transfemoral arterial pathways [1]. Approximately 10–15% of patients evaluated for transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) have iliofemoral arteries too small, tortuous, or calcified for safe transfemoral delivery [2]. Alternative access routes—including transapical, transaortic, transaxillary, transcarotid, and transcaval—have each been developed to address this challenge [3]. Transcaval access, introduced by Greenbaum and colleagues, exploits the proximity of the inferior vena cava (IVC) to the abdominal aorta, allowing a large-bore sheath to be advanced from the venous system into the aorta through an electrified guidewire crossing [4,5].

## Technique and Rationale

The transcaval technique involves deliberate puncture from the IVC into the abdominal aorta using radiofrequency energy delivered through a guidewire, typically below the renal arteries and above the aortic bifurcation [4]. Pre-procedural computed tomography is essential to identify a calcium-free target zone in the aortic wall and to confirm apposition of the cava and aorta [6]. After delivery of the large-bore device and completion of the structural intervention, the resulting aortocaval tract is closed with a nitinol occluder device deployed across the defect [5,7]. The relatively low aortic pressure gradient into the lower-pressure cava, combined with the retroperitoneal tamponade effect, often limits bleeding even before complete closure [8].

The physiological basis for transcaval access rests on the observation that aortocaval fistulae, while capable of causing bleeding, are frequently self-limiting in the retroperitoneal space [9]. Early animal studies demonstrated feasibility and reproducible closure of iatrogenic aortocaval tracts [10]. These preclinical data informed the first-in-human applications, which established proof of concept for delivering TAVR and other large-bore devices through this route [4].

## Clinical Evidence

The pivotal prospective multicenter Transcaval Access study reported a high rate of technical success in patients with no other large-bore access option, with acceptable rates of bleeding and vascular complications [11]. Subsequent registries and single-center series have confirmed favorable outcomes, with transcaval access compared favorably with surgical alternatives in several analyses [12,13]. Comparative studies have suggested that transcaval access may offer advantages over transapical and transaortic approaches by avoiding thoracotomy and direct cardiac or aortic manipulation [14,15].

Reported mortality and complication rates in contemporary cohorts have improved with operator experience and refinement of patient selection [16]. The role of computed tomographic planning in identifying optimal puncture sites and avoiding calcified or interposed bowel has been emphasized in multiple technical reports [17,18]. Several groups have documented successful use of transcaval access not only for TAVR but also for mechanical circulatory support, endovascular aneurysm repair, and transcatheter mitral interventions [19,20].

## Complications and Closure

The principal concern with transcaval access is bleeding from the aortocaval tract or from retroperitoneal extravasation [21]. Closure failure may necessitate covered stent placement or, rarely, surgical repair [22]. Dedicated nitinol occluders designed for ductal or septal closure have been adapted for transcaval tract closure, and residual aortocaval flow is commonly observed but frequently resolves over time without clinical sequelae [23,24]. Studies tracking long-term outcomes have shown that persistent fistulae are uncommon and rarely require reintervention [25]. The management of access-site complications has been incorporated into structured algorithms emphasizing prompt recognition and bailout strategies [26].

## Comparative Role and Future Directions

As transfemoral TAVR profiles continue to shrink with lower-profile delivery systems, the proportion of patients requiring alternative access has declined [27]. Nonetheless, transcaval access retains an important niche for patients with prohibitive peripheral vascular disease [28]. Comparative effectiveness data positioning transcaval access against transaxillary and transcarotid routes remain limited, and randomized data are lacking [29]. Ongoing development of purpose-built crossing and closure devices, along with standardized training pathways, may further improve safety and broaden adoption [30].

## Conclusion

Transcaval access has matured from an innovative concept into a validated alternative for large-bore structural heart interventions in carefully selected patients. With meticulous computed tomographic planning, appropriate crossing technique, and reliable closure, it offers a fully percutaneous option that avoids the morbidity of surgical chest access. Future comparative studies and dedicated device development will help define its optimal place among the expanding array of alternative access strategies.
